title: Cato Report Finds DOL Rule Raising H-1B Wages by $26,000 Likely Illegal, Would Disqualify 80% of Workers
excerpt: The Department of Labor proposed the most aggressive overhaul of H-1B prevailing wages in two decades. A detailed Cato Institute analysis argues the rule has no legal or empirical foundation.
body:
• The Department of Labor proposed a rule in March 2026 that would raise mandatory H-1B minimum wages by roughly $26,000 per year, with entry-level thresholds jumping from the 17th to 34th percentile.
  • The Cato Institute argues the rule is unlawful, would disqualify more than 80% of current H-1B wage offers, and force hundreds of thousands of existing visa holders out of the country.
  • Universities, research institutions, and healthcare employers that rely heavily on H-1B workers could face the steepest disruption, as their wages are commonly below the proposed floors.
  • The comment period closed on May 26, 2026, and a final rule could take effect within months, directly affecting an estimated 730,000 H-1B workers in the United States.

What the DOL Is Proposing

On March 27, 2026, the Department of Labor published a proposed rule that would fundamentally alter how prevailing wages are calculated for the H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, and PERM labor certification programs. The changes would raise wage floors across all four skill tiers, with entry-level requirements increasing by more than 30%.

Under the current methodology, in place since 2005, the four wage levels are pegged to the 17th, 34th, 50th, and 67th percentiles of wage data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The proposed rule would shift those to the 34th, 52nd, 70th, and 88th percentiles, respectively. For the average H-1B position, that translates to roughly $26,000 more per year in mandatory minimum pay.

"The Trump Administration is committed to ensuring that American workers are not disadvantaged by unfair wage practices," U.S. Secretary of Labor Lori Chavez-DeRemer said when the rule was published. "The continued abuse of the H-1B program by certain bad actors will no longer be tolerated."

Why Cato Says the Rule Is Unlawful

The Cato Institute, a nonpartisan policy research organization in Washington, submitted detailed comments on May 26, 2026, arguing the proposed rule has no legal or empirical foundation. David J. Bier, the institute's lead immigration researcher, wrote that DOL "provides no empirical basis for raising the prevailing wage" and that the data actually shows H-1B workers already earn wages in the top 10% nationally.

"The Department of Homeland Security separately reported that 83% of H-1B visas petitioned for between 2020 and 2024 were for entry-level and junior positions with salaries below the local median."

"The Department of Homeland Security separately reported that 83% of H-1B visas petitioned for between 2020 and 2024 were for entry-level and junior positions with salaries below the local median."

"The Department of Homeland Security separately reported that 83% of H-1B visas petitioned for between 2020 and 2024 were for entry-level and junior positions with salaries below the local median."

Cato's analysis found that more than 80% of current H-1B wage offers would be disqualified under the new thresholds — including a majority at the highest skill level, Level 4, reserved for "fully competent" workers. For software developers, the single most common H-1B occupation, the failure rate would be similarly devastating.

"The proposed rule only inflates wages to restrict the supply of skilled foreign workers beyond what the law allows and will force existing H-1B workers to leave the country."

— David J. Bier, Cato Institute

The institute argues that the current prevailing wage already aligns with actual entry-level wages. Using American Community Survey data, Cato calculated that the median wage for young H-1B-eligible workers in top occupations falls at approximately the 19th percentile — close to the current 17th percentile threshold but far below the proposed 34th. At the senior level, experienced workers with the highest required education earn at roughly the 70th percentile, nearly matching the current Level 4 threshold of 67%, but nowhere near the proposed 88%.

The Broader Battle Over H-1B

The wage rule is the latest front in an intensifying political battle over the H-1B program. The Department of Homeland Security separately reported that 83% of H-1B visas petitioned for between 2020 and 2024 were for entry-level and junior positions with salaries below the local median. Critics have seized on these numbers as evidence that the program has strayed from its original purpose of importing only the "best and brightest."

Congress added the $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions through the reconciliation process earlier this year, and the DHS published a separate regulation on July 17, 2026, ending the longstanding "duration of status" practice for international students, replacing it with fixed admission periods and mandatory extensions. Together, these actions represent the most aggressive regulatory overhaul of legal immigration in a generation.

Microsoft's recent approval to bring on 2,273 H-1B workers while laying off 4,800 existing employees intensified public anger. Even some Silicon Valley insiders, including venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, have acknowledged that the program needs reform.

What It Means for Indian Workers

Indian nationals account for roughly 72% of all H-1B approvals, making them by far the most affected group. The proposed wage floor increases would hit particularly hard in occupations dominated by Indian workers — software development, IT consulting, data analysis, and engineering — where companies have historically filed at lower wage levels.

For Indian workers already in the United States on H-1B visas, the stakes are personal. Many have been in the country for years, often while waiting in the employment-based green card backlog that stretches decades for Indian nationals. A prevailing wage increase could make their current positions untenable if employers cannot or will not raise compensation to meet new thresholds.

Universities and research institutions, which employ a significant share of H-1B holders in lower-paying but high-impact roles such as postdoctoral research and medical residencies, have pushed back strongly. The University of Michigan submitted a formal comment letter opposing the rule, arguing it is "unreasonable, unnecessary and would have a significant, negative impact on institutions of higher education."

What Comes Next

The public comment period closed on May 26, 2026. DOL must now review the comments and issue a final rule, a process that typically takes several months. The rule would not retroactively affect previously issued prevailing wage determinations. But once effective, it would reshape the economics of every new H-1B petition and PERM labor certification filed in the country.

Legal challenges are virtually certain. Cato's argument that the rule exceeds DOL's statutory authority echoes the legal reasoning that led federal courts to strike down the department's 2020 interim final rule. Whether the courts reach the same conclusion this time may depend on whether DOL can demonstrate a stronger empirical basis — something its critics say it has conspicuously failed to do.
